subject: Economics
description: Article 280, devolution, horizontal and vertical transfers, 15th FC recommendations

questions.stem: The Finance Commission of India is a constitutional body established under:

options.option_text: Article 275
Article 280
Article 356
Article 148

questions.explanation: Article 280 — the President shall, within two years of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year (or earlier as required), constitute a Finance Commission. Chairman + 4 other members, appointed by the President. Its job: recommend distribution of net tax proceeds between Centre and States (vertical) and among States (horizontal). First FC in 1951 under K.C. Neogy.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Chairman of the 15th Finance Commission (which covered 2020-21 to 2025-26) was:

options.option_text: Y.V. Reddy
N.K. Singh
C. Rangarajan
Vijay Kelkar

questions.explanation: N.K. Singh (former Bihar MP, ex-Revenue Secretary) chaired the 15th FC (2017-21). Its award covered FY 2020-21 initially, then extended to 2021-26 (six years). Reddy — 14th FC; Rangarajan — 12th FC; Kelkar — 13th FC. 16th Finance Commission was constituted in Dec 2023 under Arvind Panagariya (covers 2026-27 to 2030-31). Report due by 31 Oct 2025, implementation 1 Apr 2026.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 15th Finance Commission recommended that States' share in the net divisible pool of Central taxes be:
questions.explanation: 15th FC kept the vertical devolution at 41% (down from 14th FC's 42%, the 1 percentage point diverted to compensate for J&K losing Statehood and becoming two UTs — Centre retains the share for those UT budgets). This is higher than 13th FC (32%) and 14th FC (42%). 'Vertical' = Centre-vs-States split; 'Horizontal' = inter-State formula weighting population, area, income distance, forest cover, tax effort, demographic performance.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which factor was introduced for the first time in the 15th Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula?

options.option_text: Income distance
Demographic performance
Forest cover
Population

questions.explanation: 'Demographic performance' — a reward for lower total fertility rate — was a new 12.5% weight introduced in 15th FC. It compensates southern States for controlling their population (which otherwise lowers their share when population weight is based on latest Census). 15th FC weights: Income distance 45%, Population (2011) 15%, Area 15%, Demographic performance 12.5%, Forest cover 10%, Tax effort 2.5%.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The Chairman of the 16th Finance Commission, constituted in December 2023, is:

options.option_text: N.K. Singh
Arvind Panagariya
Urjit Patel
Bibek Debroy

questions.explanation: Dr. Arvind Panagariya — economist, former NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman (2015-17), Columbia professor — chairs the 16th FC. Members include Ajay Narayan Jha, Annie George Mathew, Manoj Panda (econ), Soumya Kanti Ghosh (part-time). Terms of Reference announced 29 Nov 2023. Report to cover five years starting 1 April 2026. Report due 31 Oct 2025.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Under the Constitution, a Finance Commission's recommendations are:

options.option_text: Binding on the Union Government
Recommendatory (advisory) in nature
Subject to approval by the Supreme Court
Binding only on State governments

questions.explanation: FC recommendations are NOT legally binding. The President lays the FC report before Parliament along with an 'Action Taken Report' explaining which recommendations are accepted. In practice, the Centre has accepted the vertical devolution formula (States' share %) and most grants recommendations from the 11th FC onwards. Grants-in-aid to States under Article 275 and devolution under Article 270 are the two main channels.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The difference between the Finance Commission and the GST Council is that:

options.option_text: FC recommends; GST Council's decisions are binding after notification
Both are purely advisory
Both are binding on Centre and States
FC is statutory; GST Council is constitutional

questions.explanation: FC (Art 280) — constitutional, recommendatory. GST Council (Art 279A, 101st Amendment, 2017) — constitutional and 'recommendatory' on paper, but Supreme Court in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) confirmed its recommendations are not binding on Parliament or State legislatures — they act as guidance. However, once accepted and notified, CGST/SGST rates are legally enforced. FC deals with revenue sharing; GST Council deals with tax rates + procedure.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Grants-in-aid to States from the Consolidated Fund of India, as recommended by the Finance Commission to assist States whose revenue is insufficient for minimum governmental needs, are governed by which constitutional article?

options.option_text: Article 280, which constitutes the Finance Commission itself
Article 282, which covers discretionary grants by Union or States
Article 293, which governs borrowing by State governments
Article 275, which provides for charged grants-in-aid to States

questions.explanation: Article 275 specifically provides for grants-in-aid charged on the Consolidated Fund of India to States whose revenue is inadequate for minimum government functions. Article 280 merely constitutes the Finance Commission. Article 282 is for discretionary grants (not tied to the FC's formal award). Article 293 deals with State borrowings from the Union.

questions.stem: Under Article 280(1) of the Constitution, the President of India is required to constitute a Finance Commission within two years of commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiry of every _____ years.

options.option_text: Three years, as amended by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act
Four years, as specified in the Finance Commission Act, 1951
Five years, as expressly stipulated under Article 280(1)
Six years, to synchronise with the medium-term fiscal framework cycle

questions.explanation: Article 280(1) mandates constitution of the Finance Commission 'within two years from the commencement of this Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year.' The 73rd Amendment deals with Panchayats, not the FC's periodicity. The Finance Commission Act 1951 governs qualifications but does not alter the five-year cycle.

questions.stem: The 14th Finance Commission (covering 2015–20) made a landmark recommendation that gave States their largest-ever share in the Central divisible pool. Which of the following correctly pairs the Chairman's name with the revised States' share?

options.option_text: Y. V. Reddy chaired; States' share was raised from 32% to 42%
N. K. Singh chaired; States' share was raised from 30% to 39%
C. Rangarajan chaired; States' share was raised from 29% to 38%
Vijay Kelkar chaired; States' share was raised from 32% to 40%

questions.explanation: The 14th Finance Commission was chaired by Y. V. Reddy (former RBI Governor) and famously raised the States' devolution share from 32% (13th FC award) to 42% — the highest in history. N. K. Singh chaired the 15th FC; Vijay Kelkar chaired the 13th FC (2010–15). C. Rangarajan has never chaired a Finance Commission.

questions.stem: In the horizontal devolution formula recommended by the 15th Finance Commission, which single criterion carried the highest weight, reflecting the Commission's emphasis on inter-State fiscal equalisation?

options.option_text: Population based on 2011 Census data, assigned 15% weight in formula
Income distance from the richest State's per capita GSDP, weighted at 45%
Geographical area of the State, assigned a weight of 15% in the formula
Demographic performance on fertility control, weighted at 12.5% in formula

questions.explanation: Income distance (45%) was the dominant criterion in the 15th FC horizontal formula, designed to transfer more resources to poorer States as an equalisation measure. The complete formula: income distance 45%, population (2011) 15%, area 15%, demographic performance 12.5%, forest and ecology 10%, tax and fiscal effort 2.5%. Options A, C, D are real criteria but each carries far lower weight.

questions.stem: The 13th Finance Commission (2010–15) was notable for, among other things, linking fiscal incentive grants to States' compliance with FRBM-type fiscal consolidation targets. Who chaired this Commission?

options.option_text: Y. V. Reddy, former Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
C. Rangarajan, former Chairman of the PM's Economic Advisory Council
Bimal Jalan, former Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
Vijay Kelkar, former Finance Secretary and tax reform architect

questions.explanation: Vijay Kelkar chaired the 13th Finance Commission (2010–15). It was the first to explicitly tie grants to fiscal performance metrics aligned with FRBM targets — a template later followed by the 14th and 15th FCs. Y. V. Reddy chaired the 14th FC; N. K. Singh chaired the 15th FC. Bimal Jalan has not chaired any Finance Commission, making him the most tempting but incorrect distractor.

questions.stem: The 15th Finance Commission extended 'Revenue Deficit Grants' (post-devolution) to select States for each year of its award period. What was the determining criterion for a State's eligibility for these grants in a given year?

options.option_text: Post-devolution projected revenue expenditure exceeded the State's revenue receipts
The State's own tax-to-GSDP ratio fell below the national median in the base year
The State held 'special category' status as certified by the Inter-State Council
The State's fiscal deficit exceeded 3.5% of GSDP in two consecutive preceding years

questions.explanation: Revenue Deficit Grants bridge the gap when a State's normatively assessed revenue expenditure exceeds its projected revenue receipts (own taxes + non-tax revenue + devolution share). Only States with a negative post-devolution revenue balance become eligible. Option B relates to tax effort (a devolution criterion, not grant eligibility). Option C confuses 'special category' status — a Planning Commission concept not used by the 15th FC. Option D describes a fiscal-deficit threshold, which governs borrowing limits, not Revenue Deficit Grant eligibility.

questions.stem: The constitutional distinction between grants under Article 275 and grants under Article 282 carries significant fiscal implications for Centre-State transfers. Which of the following most precisely captures this distinction?

options.option_text: Article 275 funds capital expenditure only; Article 282 funds revenue expenditure
Article 275 grants are limited to special category States; Article 282 covers all States
Article 275 grants are charged on the Consolidated Fund; Article 282 grants are voted
Article 275 is a Finance Commission instrument; Article 282 needs Planning Commission nod

questions.explanation: Article 275 grants are 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India, meaning they are automatically available without an annual parliamentary vote — they are non-votable appropriations. Article 282 grants are discretionary and require annual parliamentary appropriation (voted expenditure). Option A is factually wrong — both articles can fund revenue or capital needs. Option B is incorrect; Article 275 is not restricted to special category States. Option D is partly true (275 flows from FC award) but the 'Planning Commission nod' for Article 282 is wrong — the Planning Commission was dissolved in 2014.
